sections.learningObjectives:
- Apply correct collection timing for fasting, timed, trough/peak, first-morning, and stat specimens in accordance with clinician orders and office policy.
- Maintain required transport and storage conditions, including temperature, light protection, and container integrity, to preserve specimens in transit and in storage.
- Preserve specimen integrity by following processing, mixing, separation, and stability requirements and by recognizing conditions that degrade specimens.
- Escalate collection timing, transport, and storage problems to appropriate staff following office policy and the chain of command.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Timing for a lab test is like a recipe that says 'check the cake at exactly 40 minutes.' If you check too early or too late, the answer you get is wrong, so the helper follows the timer exactly.

### Question 2

Fasting is like clearing your plate before a contest. You leave everything out except plain water, so the test shows the clean, resting level of what the doctor wants to measure.

### Question 3

It is like noticing a racer started before the whistle. The helper tells the referee instead of pretending the race was fair, because a false start ruins the result.

### Question 4

Think of the first morning urine like the strongest cup of tea made from the same bag. It has been sitting and concentrating all night, so clues show up more clearly.

### Question 5

It is like filling a rain gauge for one full day. You empty it at the start, note the time, and then catch every drop for the next 24 hours, right up to the finish.

### Question 6

Keeping the collection jug cold and covered is like putting leftovers in the fridge with the lid on so they stay good until you are ready to use them.

### Question 7

A trough is the valley between hills. You measure it right before the next dose, when the medicine level has dipped to its lowest point.

### Question 8

The peak is the top of the hill, and every medicine reaches it at a different moment. If you do not know the moment, you ask the person who ordered the test instead of guessing.

### Question 9

If someone already climbed the hill before you measured the valley, you tell the coach what really happened instead of pretending you measured a valley.

### Question 10

Recording the time is like putting a timestamp on a photo of a race; without it, no one can tell what moment the picture shows.

### Question 11

STAT is like a fire alarm; you do not wait for a full bus. You send that one right away.

### Question 12

Cortisol is like a morning alarm in the body: it naturally turns up high in the early morning, so that is when the doctor samples it.

### Question 13

It is like checking a sand timer two hours after you flip it at the start of a meal, to see how well the body cleared the sugar.

### Question 14

It is like checking a ball rolling downhill at several marked spots, so the doctor can see the whole path, not just one point.

### Question 15

A1c is like a report card of your average sugar over the last few months, so it does not matter what you ate this morning.

### Question 16

If you are not sure the cookie jar was left untouched, you ask before labeling the jar 'untouched.'

### Question 17

It is like catching a bug in a jar before you spray the garden; once the spray (antibiotic) is out, the bug is much harder to find.

### Question 18

A random sample is like scooping a cup of water any time, while a timed sample is like collecting rain for an exact hour.

### Question 19

The helper tells the patient exactly how long to leave the plate empty and that plain water is okay, so the test is fair for everyone.

### Question 20

If you miss the exact second to start a race, you tell the official and ask whether to restart, rather than pretending the start was perfect.

### Question 21

The trough is the lowest dip between waves; the doctor checks the dip to be sure the medicine never drops too low or piles up too high.

### Question 22

Keeping a specimen cold is like keeping ice cream cold without letting it freeze into a solid block if the recipe says 'keep chilled, not frozen.'

### Question 23

A specimen is like a carton of milk; if it rides around warm too long, it spoils, and the measurement is no longer trustworthy.

### Question 24

It is like carrying a cold drink in a lunchbox with an ice pack so it stays chilled and the box does not leak.

### Question 25

It is like keeping an ice cube frozen by carrying it in a cooler with dry ice, not in your pocket.

### Question 26

Some things, like certain houseplants, are happiest at room temperature and get hurt in the fridge; some lab samples are the same.

### Question 27

A STAT sample is like a phone call to 911; you do not wait for a scheduled time, you send it right now.

### Question 28

It is like putting a juice box inside a sealed plastic bag before it goes in the backpack, so a leak does not make a mess.

### Question 29

It is like standing bottles up in a crate so they do not tip over and spill on the ride.

### Question 30

Bilirubin is like a photograph that fades in bright light, so you keep it covered so the true amount is not lost.

### Question 31

It is like covering a bowl of leftovers with foil so the air and light cannot change it before it arrives.

### Question 32

If the delivery truck is missed for a package of ice cream, you call to arrange a new ride before it melts, not wait until tomorrow.

### Question 33

A specimen is like a cut apple; leave it on the counter and it keeps changing color until it no longer looks like it did at the start.

### Question 34

It is like straining the broth from the vegetables so the vegetables stop flavoring the soup while it waits.

### Question 35

Red blood cells are like tiny water balloons; shake them too hard and they pop, spilling their contents into the sample.

### Question 36

If the ice cream melts and you refreeze it, it is never quite the same; you tell the person in charge instead of pretending it never melted.

### Question 37

Putting the sample on ice is like slowing down a tiny engine inside the blood so the gases stay the same until the lab reads them.

### Question 38

Hand-carrying is like personally delivering an urgent package when the regular truck already left, and signing the log so everyone knows who has it.

### Question 39

The transport medium is like a little lunchbox of nutrients that keeps the germs alive on the trip to the lab.

### Question 40

A leaking tube is like a cracked juice box; you put it in a sealed bag with gloves on and tell an adult, instead of letting it drip.

### Question 41

It is like a thermos for the sample, keeping hot things hot or cold things cold while it travels.

### Question 42

A specimen is like milk with a sell-by date; after that time, you cannot trust it for the recipe.

### Question 43

The specimen fridge is like a normal refrigerator that keeps food at a safe, cool temperature — not frozen, not warm.

### Question 44

If the fridge is too warm, you tell the person in charge instead of writing down a pretend temperature.

### Question 45

The specimen fridge is like the science-lab fridge; you would not put your sandwich next to lab samples, and you would not put samples next to food.

### Question 46

Frozen samples live in a deep-freeze, like ice cream kept rock solid, not in the regular fridge.

### Question 47

Freezing whole blood is like freezing a water balloon; the ice expands and pops it.

### Question 48

Once you strain the soup from the vegetables, you can keep the broth in the fridge or freezer depending on how long it must last.

### Question 49

Putting the urine in the fridge is like refrigerating leftovers so they stay good until you can use them.

### Question 50

Checking the fridge temperature every day is like checking the smoke alarm battery, so you catch a problem before something is ruined.

### Question 51

It is like cramming too many items into a fridge so the cold air cannot move around them, and some things stay warm.

### Question 52

A specimen has a 'best before' time like food; after that, the numbers it gives are no longer trustworthy.

### Question 53

If the leftovers sat too long, you throw them out and start over rather than serving them with a new date.

### Question 54

Standing bottles upright in a rack is like storing them so they do not tip, leak, or hide their labels.

### Question 55

Keep light-sensitive samples covered like film for a camera, so light does not ruin them before they are read.

### Question 56

The swab in its medium is like a seed in a damp packet; you keep it at the right temperature and covered until planting time.

### Question 57

Some germs are like tropical plants that do not like the cold, so they stay at room temperature to stay alive.

### Question 58

Specimens wait in a special holding spot, like mail in a locked box, away from food and busy hands.

### Question 59

40 °F is about 4 °C — like a normal cold fridge, which is exactly where these samples belong.

### Question 60

Rotation is like using the oldest milk first so nothing goes past its date.

### Question 61

The blood cells are still 'eating' the sugar while the tube waits, so the longer it sits, the less sugar is left to measure.

### Question 62

Potassium is like salt packed inside the cells; if you wait too long, it leaks out into the liquid around the cells and makes it look saltier than it really is.

### Question 63

Hemolysis is when the little red balloons pop and leak their red coloring into the liquid.

### Question 64

Treat the sample gently, like carrying eggs; shaking it hard or squeezing it through a tiny straw breaks the cells.

### Question 65

Mix additive tubes like gently turning a bottle of juice to mix the pulp, not like shaking a can of soda.

### Question 66

The tube is like a recipe that needs a set amount of ingredients; too little blood spoils the ratio and the result.

### Question 67

Moving blood from one tube to another is like pouring juice between glasses; you spill, mix flavors, and risk mislabeling.

### Question 68

A clot is like a lump in the batter; you do not serve it, you start that sample over.

### Question 69

The cells keep working and leaking while they wait, like fruit continuing to ripen and soften on the counter.

### Question 70

Spinning the tube separates the clear liquid from the cells, like straining soup before the vegetables change the broth.

### Question 71

Each tube is like a labeled container with a special ingredient inside; using the wrong one ruins the recipe.

### Question 72

Keep the lid on the collection jug, like capping a water bottle, so nothing extra falls in.

### Question 73

The assistant is like the careful courier and record-keeper who follows the plan and calls for help when something is off, not the one who writes the plan.

### Question 74

Treat every specimen like it could carry germs, so you wear gloves and wash your hands every time, just like before handling food.

### Question 75

The biohazard sign is like a 'wet floor' warning that tells everyone to be careful before they touch it.

### Question 76

A spill is cleaned like any mess that could carry germs: gloves on, wipe it safely with cleaner, and tell the person in charge.

### Question 77

A specimen without a name is like a letter with no address; you do not guess the address, you start over with a new label.

### Question 78

Using the wrong container is like baking in the wrong pan; you start over with the right one instead of just renaming it.

### Question 79

You never fill in a pretend answer on a log; you tell the person in charge the log was missed and check the real temperature.

### Question 80

When you find a problem, you tell the person in charge and follow the rules, like reporting a spill to a teacher.

### Question 81

Writing down something that did not happen is like cheating on a test; it breaks trust and can harm someone.

### Question 82

If the soup spoiled on the way, you do not relabel it with an old date; you give the patient a fresh container and clear directions.

### Question 83

The specimen fridge is only for specimens; finding food in it is like finding a sandwich in the science lab and telling the teacher.

### Question 84

If the power went out, you check how long the fridge was off and ask the person in charge whether the contents are still safe, instead of guessing.

### Question 85

A specimen belongs in its special sealed case, not in a pocket, just like you would not carry an open cup of water in your coat.
